title: The doorway effect: why did I come in here?
description: Walk into a room and forget what you wanted? Discover the doorway effect, why a change of scene may matter, and why the science is not so simple.

sections.title: A room, a mission, a blank
sections.html:
You head into another room for your keys. At the doorway, the mission goes missing. The keys, annoyingly, have not volunteered their location.

The doorway effect describes a pattern found in some experiments: crossing into another room can make recently encountered information harder to recall. Notre Dame researchers reported it in virtual and real rooms.

sections.title: A change of scene may matter
sections.html:
One explanation involves event boundaries. We organise experience into episodes; a new room can mark the start of another one. Information from the previous episode may become less accessible.

Think of a scene change in a film. That is a helpful comparison, not evidence that your brain presses a delete button whenever a door opens.

sections.title: Not every door does it
sections.html:
A 2021 study with four experiments found no overall increase in forgetting after doorways. When people also had a demanding counting task, researchers did find more confusion between remembered items.

A 2026 word-list study tested a different question: could learning across two rooms help? It found little overall benefit, with a brief advantage near the doorway in one experiment. The task and timing matter.

sections.title: Keep the curiosity
sections.html:
It is a memorable name for an interesting research question, rather than a complete explanation for every lost thought.

For more memory surprises, explore why the start and end of a list stand out, or see how familiar groups make information easier to handle. Your keys can have another moment in the spotlight afterwards.
